wrong-normal-reference.reason: It looks like the angle was measured from the mirror surface instead of from the normal. Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured from the normal line.
wrong-normal-reference.focus_area: Show the normal at the point of incidence and mark both angles from that line.

angle-addition-confusion.reason: The answer suggests you tried to add or subtract angles instead of using the simple rule i = r.
angle-addition-confusion.focus_area: Highlight the two equal angles on either side of the normal.

incidence-plus-reflection.reason: It seems you treated the sum of the angles as important, but the law of reflection only says each angle is equal to the other.
incidence-plus-reflection.focus_area: Emphasise that angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, not their sum.

normal-incidence-misread.reason: When light hits the mirror along the normal, it retraces its path. The ray does not bend away; it goes straight back.
normal-incidence-misread.focus_area: Show the incident ray along the normal and the reflected ray on top of it.

reflection-refraction-mixup.reason: This choice mixes up reflection (bouncing off a surface) with refraction (bending in a new medium).
reflection-refraction-mixup.focus_area: Contrast a ray bouncing from a mirror with a ray bending at a glass surface.

mirror-absorption-myth.reason: A plane mirror mostly reflects light; it does not "use up" or absorb all the light in this context.
mirror-absorption-myth.focus_area: Show many rays bouncing off the mirror to show reflection.

frequency-change-myth.reason: The frequency of light does not change when it enters a new medium; only its speed and wavelength change.
frequency-change-myth.focus_area: Highlight that f stays the same while speed and wavelength change in the second medium.

wavelength-direction-mixup.reason: The answer suggests confusion between how wavelength changes and how the ray bends at the boundary.
wavelength-direction-mixup.focus_area: Link the change in ray direction with the change in wavelength inside the new medium.

material-emission-misconception.reason: The glass or lens does not create extra light in this situation; it only bends the light passing through.
material-emission-misconception.focus_area: Show rays entering and leaving the material without any new rays being created.

real-vs-virtual-confusion.reason: This choice mixes up when images are real (can be caught on a screen) and when they are virtual.
real-vs-virtual-confusion.focus_area: Show a ray diagram with real image on a screen versus a virtual image behind a mirror or lens.

optical-center-myth.reason: The optical centre is not the only place where an object can form a real image. The object position relative to the focal length matters.
optical-center-myth.focus_area: Highlight the focal points and different object positions around the lens.

infinity-only-myth.reason: A convex lens can form a real image for many object positions beyond the focal length, not just at infinity.
infinity-only-myth.focus_area: Show several object positions beyond the focal length and their image locations.

general_concept_gap.reason: Your pattern of answers suggests a general gap in this concept rather than one specific mistake.
general_concept_gap.focus_area: Redo the main animation or diagram slowly, pausing at each step.

no_concept.reason: It looks like the core idea for this question is unclear. Start from the definition and key law, then apply it to the example.
no_concept.focus_area: Show the single diagram or formula that the question is based on.
